title: Automotive Parts & Accessories Association v. Boyd (1968)
shortTitle: Automotive Parts & Accessories Association v. Boyd (1968)
summary: An informal safety rule must explain the major issues and the agency’s responses; the court sustained mandatory factory-installed head restraints.

sections.Parties: Sterling Products, a maker of automobile accessories, and two industry associations challenged the Secretary of Transportation’s head-restraint standard. Their members sold aftermarket accessories and stood to lose sales when manufacturers installed restraints at the factory.
sections.Material Facts: Standard No. 202 required new passenger cars to leave the factory with front-seat head restraints beginning January 1, 1969. The challengers supported head restraints as safety devices but urged an equipment standard that would preserve consumer choice and independent suppliers. They predicted higher prices, reduced competition, slower innovation, and fewer design choices under factory installation. The agency responded that an equipment-only standard would not ensure installation in every vehicle, that restraint performance depended on the seat and its anchorage, and that a performance standard allowed integrated designs as well as add-on devices.
sections.Procedural History: The agency issued successive proposals, received written comments, held a meeting with interested parties, promulgated the standard, and denied reconsideration with an explanatory letter. The manufacturers and associations then filed consolidated petitions for direct judicial review in the D.C. Circuit. Although they had not raised their formal-hearing objection before the agency, the court addressed it because the government argued the merits and effective administration of the new statute favored a decision.
sections.Issue: Did the Safety Act require trial-type rulemaking under APA §§ 556–557, and did the agency adequately explain and substantiate its choice of mandatory factory installation under §§ 553 and 706?
sections.Holding: The court denied the petitions. Informal notice-and-comment procedures were permissible, and the agency’s explanation and supporting record sustained the standard. A requirement to lodge a record for judicial review did not itself require a formal evidentiary hearing.
sections.Reasoning: The statute’s history, its provisions for research and informal consultation, and the policy character of standard-setting supported informal procedure. A record existed in the comments and supporting materials even without trial testimony. The court nonetheless read the concise statement of basis and purpose in light of meaningful judicial review: the agency must identify the major policy issues and explain how it resolved them; a court should not reconstruct that reasoning from scattered materials. The preamble and reconsideration letter supplied adequate reasons here. Factory installation improved enforceability and universal protection, and expert materials supported the relationship between the restraint and the seat. The agency could reasonably weigh those benefits against commercial harm. The challengers’ late attack on the safety value of restraints conflicted with their earlier position, and the record independently supported the agency’s safety judgment.
